analysis.one_liner: Creates a federally guaranteed basic health insurance plan with premiums scaled to income and wealth.
analysis.headline: A bill for universal health insurance with no cosponsors died in two House committees without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Rep. Donald J. Pease introduced the Universal Health Insurance Act of 1991, which would have made a government-structured "Basic Health Insurance" available to every legal resident through qualified insurance carriers, with premiums that rise with income and net assets and a 6% payroll tax on employers who do not offer qualifying coverage. It was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees, then to their health subcommittees. It gained no cosponsors, was never reported out of committee, and never received a floor vote before the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.who_benefits: Every legal resident of the United States who lacks affordable health coverage — the bill guarantees enrollment in a basic plan with standard benefits including maternity, prenatal, and postnatal care and catastrophic coverage, with premiums set by a formula that rises with a person's income and net assets, so wealthier enrollees pay more and lower-income people pay less. People with pre-existing conditions would benefit because eligibility is universal and not conditioned on health status.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a new "Basic Health Insurance" program under a Title XXI of the Social Security Act, open to every individual legally residing in a service area, regardless of health status.

Premiums are set by a formula that takes into account an individual's income and net assets, so the premium increases with a person's wealth — meaning lower-income enrollees pay less than wealthier ones.
The benefit standards must include coverage of the types normally provided by health insurance plans, including maternity, prenatal, and postnatal care and catastrophic coverage.
Employers who do not offer employees a health plan meeting the benefit standards pay a 6% excise tax on total wages paid, creating a strong incentive for employers to provide coverage.
The program's design encourages individuals who do not otherwise have health insurance to enroll.

analysis.who_pays: Wealthier enrollees, who pay premiums that increase with income and net assets; employers who do not offer qualifying health plans, who pay a 6% excise tax on total wages; and, given the bill's tobacco-tax subject listing, tobacco consumers, who would bear part of the program's funding through cigarette and tobacco taxes.
analysis.who_pays_short: Wealthy enrollees, non-offering employers, tobacco consumers

drawbacks.text: The premium formula bases what people pay on income and net assets, meaning some middle-income families with significant assets would pay meaningfully more than under flat-rate coverage.

The 6% payroll excise tax on employers who do not offer qualifying coverage would raise the cost of employing workers without insurance, a cost that could show up as slower wage growth or fewer hires at affected firms.
Funding tied to cigarette and tobacco taxes would be regressive, falling hardest on lower-income smokers — a tradeoff supporters of tobacco-tax-funded health programs generally acknowledge.
The bill took effect only for calendar years after 1991, so even if enacted, coverage would have taken years to phase in.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have guaranteed coverage to everyone — including people priced out or turned down by insurers — paid for progressively through income- and asset-based premiums, an employer payroll tax on firms that do not cover workers, and tobacco taxes. The main costs fall on wealthier enrollees, non-offering employers, and smokers, and an honest supporter would concede the payroll tax adds a real cost of employment and the tobacco tax is regressive. On balance, the upside for the roughly tens of millions of uninsured Americans in 1991 was large relative to those costs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and then to their health subcommittees, never gained a single cosponsor, and sat without a markup or floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Donald J. Pease introduced the bill in the House on March 5, 1991.
On the day of introduction it was referred to both the House Committee on Energy and Commerce and the House Committee on Ways and Means.
Within two weeks it was referred to the health subcommittees of those committees (Subcommittee on Health; Subcommittee on Health and the Environment), the normal first stop for health bills.
The bill drew zero cosponsors for the entire two-year Congress.
No further action was recorded, and the bill died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, without any committee vote or floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who do not provide health insurance were better off because the 6% wage excise tax never took effect; health insurers avoided a government-structured, income-based public alternative that would have competed with or regulated their market; and the tobacco industry avoided the new cigarette and tobacco taxes listed among the bill's funding subjects. Uninsured Americans got nothing.

for.name: Rep. Donald J. Pease
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Universal Health Insurance Act of 1991 and was its only sponsor for the life of the bill.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and passed it to the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment; never reported the bill or scheduled a markup.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and passed it to the Subcommittee on Health; never reported the bill or scheduled a markup.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no party split is on record; it had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, and no Republican took a recorded position on it.

industries.note: The bill routes the universal basic plan through "qualified" private insurance carriers, which would have locked carriers in as the permanent administrators of the program — but under government-set benefit standards, universal eligibility, and premiums regulated by income and wealth, which also creates a cheaper, guaranteed alternative to conventional insurance. Insurers had an interest in keeping the bill off the table.

Any employer that did not offer a plan meeting the bill's benefit standards would owe a 6% excise tax on total wages paid, a direct new payroll cost. Employer groups historically opposed payroll-tax-based health mandates.

Cigarette and tobacco taxes appear among the bill's subjects as part of its funding, meaning a new or higher tobacco excise would help pay for the program — a cost borne by tobacco companies' customers and revenues.
